paragraphs: The central problem is **working backwards from a fluorescent movie to the neural processes that could have produced it**. Avitan’s published work gives us concrete examples of the methods and software. The tutorial alone does not identify her current simulator.

In her published zebrafish experiments, neurons express **GCaMP6s**, a protein whose fluorescence changes when calcium binds. Neural activity changes calcium inside a cell; a microscope records fluorescence; image analysis identifies cells and extracts a brightness trace for each one. Calcium and the indicator respond and decay over time, so the trace is a filtered, noisy measurement of activity. It does not give exact spike times directly. One 2020 experiment recorded the optic tectum, a visual brain region, at about 2.16 frames per second using two-photon microscopy. [Experimental methods](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1008330)
Two published projects illustrate different goals:

| Work | Scientific goal | Model and tools |
|---|---|---|
| **Triplett, Avitan and Goodhill (2018)** | Explain how groups of neurons develop coordinated activity without structured external input. | A **MATLAB circuit simulation**. Its default is 125 simplified neurons, each active or inactive, followed over 120,000 time steps. Connections change according to activity. |
| **Triplett et al. (2020), CILVA** | Estimate which fluorescence changes follow a visual stimulus and which reflect shared spontaneous activity, under the model’s assumptions. | A **Python model using NumPy for array calculations and SciPy for optimization**. It combines stimulus effects and hidden shared signals, then models calcium rise, decay and measurement noise. |

The first generates developing circuit activity; the second fits recorded fluorescence. CILVA’s hidden-signal contributions are not an anatomical map of connections between neurons. These are published examples, not an identification of the model she currently runs. [2018 paper and MATLAB code](https://github.com/marcustriplett/assembly_formation_model), [CILVA paper](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1008330), [CILVA code](https://github.com/GoodhillLab/CILVA)

**The sbi tutorial adds a way to estimate model parameters from observations.** In its neural posterior estimation method, an artificial neural network learns from examples produced by a simulator. That inference network is separate from the model of the fish circuit.
For a possible zebrafish application, one complete cycle would be:

1. Choose a **prior**, a distribution over parameter settings before using the observed recording. The parameters might describe connection strength, background activity or response times; the actual choices depend on the circuit model.
2. Draw settings from that distribution and run the circuit simulation.
3. Convert the resulting activity into fluorescence, or into measurements comparable with those extracted from the experiment. Store each setting together with its output.
4. Train the inference network on those pairs. Present the real measurements to obtain an **approximate posterior**, a distribution over settings given those measurements and the assumed model and prior.
5. Draw settings from that posterior, simulate again, and check whether their outputs reproduce the observed behavior.

The supplied tutorial demonstrates this with a small Gaussian example. It allows the scientific simulations to run separately, including in another programming language, before their outputs enter Python/PyTorch. [sbi tutorial, v0.23.2](https://sbi-dev.github.io/sbi/v0.23.2/tutorials/00_getting_started/)

Agreement with recordings does not establish a unique biological circuit. Several parameter choices or model structures can fit similar measurements. These additional simulations check what the fitted model predicts. [Predictive checks](https://sbi-dev.github.io/sbi/v0.23.2/tutorials/10_diagnostics_posterior_predictive_checks/)
**GPU acceleration depends on which operation consumes the time.** I would measure movie-to-trace extraction, circuit/fluorescence simulation, inference-network training, and validation separately.

| Work consuming time | Improvement to investigate |
|---|---|
| Many independent small simulations | Run several at once on CPU cores; compare this with GPU execution. |
| Large or numerous similar array calculations | Try GPU **batching**: carry out the same operations for many simulations together, keeping their data on the GPU. |
| Repeated calculations over long fluorescence traces | Change the numerical algorithm before deciding whether a GPU is needed. |
| Inference-network training | Test PyTorch on CPU and GPU. Small networks may run just as fast on CPU. |
| Too many parameter trials | Use more targeted simulation rounds, or reuse a trained inference network across recordings. |

Setting sbi’s training device to CUDA does not move the scientific simulator onto the GPU. Its parallel simulation helper uses CPU worker processes. The v0.23.2 maintainers also say their default small inference networks may gain no speed from GPU training. [Versioned GPU guidance](https://github.com/sbi-dev/sbi/blob/v0.23.2/docs/docs/faq/question_04_gpu.md), [simulation helper](https://github.com/sbi-dev/sbi/blob/v0.23.2/sbi/utils/simulation_utils.py)

There is already **one concrete opportunity in the public CILVA code**. It repeatedly recomputes the calcium response across an entire recording. Its particular rise-and-decay formula can instead be updated recursively: keep two running responses, one fast and one slow, update each with the new activity, and take their difference. This can reduce that filtering work from roughly quadratic to linear in recording length. I checked the equivalent calculation on synthetic traces, including the calculation used during fitting. That establishes numerical agreement for this operation, not a measured speedup for the complete fit or her current project. [Inspected source](https://github.com/GoodhillLab/CILVA/blob/master/cilva/core.py)

Reducing the number of runs is a separate option. **Sequential SBI** repeats simulation and fitting, using each round to target the next simulations toward one observation. A broadly trained inference network can instead be reused across many recordings. Which saves more time depends on whether the project studies one recording or many, and neither guarantees a shorter total run. [Sequential and reusable inference](https://sbi-dev.github.io/sbi/v0.23.2/tutorials/02_multiround_inference/)

Your computer has an **i7-13700H and an RTX 4050 Laptop GPU with about 6 GB of GPU memory**. It is a reasonable machine for testing moderate models and comparing CPU and GPU approaches; the actual array sizes determine what fits.

The next useful material from her is **one runnable example**, together with the parameters it varies, the data it returns, and its typical runtime. That would let us identify the slow operation, make one targeted change, and compare runtime, memory use and the scientific quantities being estimated. I have not run her simulator or measured an end-to-end GPU speedup.
